linkedin.title: Flight delayed or cancelled? What Canadian passengers can claim
linkedin.caption:
Holiday travel season is almost here. If your flight is delayed or cancelled, it may not just be bad luck.

Under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations, a large airline owes compensation when a delay is within its control and not required for safety:
• Arrive 3 to under 6 hours late: $400
• 6 to under 9 hours late: $700
• 9 hours or more: $1,000
Small airlines pay lower amounts. If a flight is cancelled, you can be rebooked or refunded.

1. Keep your boarding pass, receipts and airline messages.
2. Send your claim to the airline in writing.
3. Claim within one year of the flight.
4. If the airline hasn't fixed it after 30 days, file a free complaint with the Canadian Transportation Agency. The backlog is large, so file early.

linkedin.title: Dealing with a debt collector? Your rights in Canada
linkedin.caption:
Collection calls are stressful, but collection agencies are licensed and regulated by each province. Generally, they are not allowed to:
• Call very early or very late
• Contact your workplace after you've told them not to
• Threaten action they won't take
• Use abusive language
• Tell others about your debt

What to do:
1. Ask for the agency's name and licence number, and check your province's collection agency registry before sharing any information.
2. Keep a log of every call.
3. Tell them in writing that they may contact you only by mail. Most provinces then require them to use mail or go through a lawyer. The debt itself doesn't go away.
4. Report rule-breaking to your provincial consumer protection office. In Ontario, that's Consumer Protection Ontario.

If it's your bank's own collections department, raise it with the bank first, then the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada.

linkedin.title: Owed money? Small claims court limits across Canada

Small claims court is designed for people without a lawyer, and the limits are higher than many people think:
• Ontario: $50,000 (since October 1, 2025)
• Alberta: $100,000, the highest in Canada
• British Columbia: up to $5,000 at the online Civil Resolution Tribunal, and $5,001 to $35,000 at Provincial Court

2. Gather your proof: contract, invoices, messages, photos.
3. If they don't pay, file your claim with your province's small claims court.

If there's a free ombudsman or regulator for your dispute, try that first. Small claims makes sense once that's exhausted.

Guide: https://www.complaintca.ca/guides/small-claims-court-canada-guide.html

linkedin.title: Problem with your Canada Student Loan? How to escalate
linkedin.caption:
There's no dedicated ombudsman for Canada Student Loans, which leaves many borrowers stuck when a payment isn't applied or a balance looks wrong. The route that works:

1. Contact the National Student Loans Service Centre (NSLSC) through the secure messaging system in your online account, or call 1-888-815-4514.
2. Document everything: account statements and every message you send. The NSLSC doesn't publish a public email address, so keep copies.
3. If it's unresolved, escalate to Service Canada / ESDC, which oversees the NSLSC.
4. Your MP's office can also request a status update on a stuck file.

In Quebec, student aid is run by Aide financière aux études (AFE), so complaints go there instead.

Guide: https://www.complaintca.ca/guides/student-loan-complaint-canada-guide.html

linkedin.title: Workers' compensation claim denied? How appeals work in Canada
linkedin.caption:
A denied workers' compensation claim can be appealed, but each province has its own steps and deadlines:

• Ontario: file an Intent to Object with the WSIB, then appeal to WSIAT within 6 months of the final decision.
• British Columbia: WorkSafeBC's Review Division first, then WCAT as the final level.
• Alberta: WCB-Alberta's Dispute Resolution and Decision Review Body, then the Appeals Commission. The Office of the Appeals Advisor gives free help.
• Quebec: ask the CNESST for an administrative review within 30 days, then contest at the Tribunal administratif du travail within 45 days.

Whatever the province: get the decision in writing, collect medical records, and don't miss the deadline.

Guide: https://www.complaintca.ca/guides/workers-compensation-complaint-canada-guide.html
